Optimized filter performance even under changing process conditions 
Filtration cycles are traditionally controlled by recipes divided into different subroutines. With 
multiple parameters to take into account, it can be challenging to correctly adjust the ﬁltration 
process to address changes in slurry characteristics or ﬁlter media condition. Filter performance is traditionally evaluated through laboratory samples and by monitoring 
cake weight. Because samples are typically collected only once per shift or even less 
frequently, operators cannot respond immediately to process changes; these can be rapid, 
such as changes in slurry density, or slow, such as ﬁlter-cloth clogging. The Metso Filter optimizer application calculates new setpoints for the most important 
subroutines cycle by cycle based on changes in ﬁlter performance. Maximized productivity with minimal manual input  
Each cake is measured after discharge and new setpoints calculated based on residual 
moisture and cycle time, optimizing the ﬁlter cycle.

separation process with a patent pending algorithm.

Automated moisture sampling and 
parameter adjustment on every cycle reduce the need for manual input from operators and

•	 Improved process visibility

How does it work?

Optimized filter performance even under changing process conditions 
Filtration cycles are traditionally controlled by recipes divided into different subroutines. With 
multiple parameters to take into account, it can be challenging to correctly adjust the ﬁltration 
process to address changes in slurry characteristics or ﬁlter media condition. Filter performance is traditionally evaluated through laboratory samples and by monitoring 
cake weight. Because samples are typically collected only once per shift or even less 
frequently, operators cannot respond immediately to process changes; these can be rapid, 
such as changes in slurry density, or slow, such as ﬁlter-cloth clogging. The Metso Filter optimizer application calculates new setpoints for the most important 
subroutines cycle by cycle based on changes in ﬁlter performance. Maximized productivity with minimal manual input  
Each cake is measured after discharge and new setpoints calculated based on residual 
moisture and cycle time, optimizing the ﬁlter cycle.

data_requests.data: Operator / control-system logs: timestamped amina and starch setpoint changes, manual vs automatic mode, who changed them and why
data_requests.why: Tests whether dosing is really reactive. Our data only shows silica leading amina in time; logs show when dosing decisions were actually made.

data_requests.data: Lab sampling times vs result reporting times for concentrate silica (and online analyser data, if any)
data_requests.why: The 3-hour lead could partly be reporting delay. Separating sample time from report time shows how late the operators' information really is.

data_requests.data: The customer's own hourly data for several months, with the same columns (feed and concentrate Fe/Si, reagent flows, pH, density, air flow, levels)
data_requests.why: The benchmark is a different plant. Their data tells us whether their 3.1% Si / 64.5% Fe is normal for their feed and whether the same timing pattern exists.
Without tailings we cannot compute recovery or mass yield, so we cannot say whether a higher grade would cost recovery.

data_requests.data: Ore characteristics: particle size (e.g. P80), mineralogy / liberation, slimes or clay content, feed rate
data_requests.why: Feed silica alone does not explain concentrate quality. These are the usual confounders we could not control for.

data_requests.data: Reagent and water details: amina and starch concentration and preparation, supplier batch, water quality and temperature
data_requests.why: Dosing flow alone ignores reagent strength and conditions, which change what a given flow does.

data_requests.data: Higher-frequency data (e.g. 20-second or 1-minute) and equipment events (downtime, maintenance)
data_requests.why: Needed to look for a leading indicator that moves hours before silica does.
